notes.text: At that time — There shall be tidings brought both to the country and city. A dry wind - A drying wind, such as shall blast and scorch where it comes, without any rain or moisture. It points at the stormy and furious irruption of the Babylonian army. In the plain - Where there is no stop in the way to break its fury. Toward - Directly, and designedly, coming in the way leading to my people. Not - Not such a gentle wind, as is made choice of to separate the chaff from the wheat; but so boisterous and violent, that it shall sweep away, and lay waste, all together.
Full — Hebrew. Fuller than they. A wind too strong for them. Shall come - It shall presently come to me, to receive my commission, and do my will.

I beheld — I Jeremiah saw this in a vision. It - The land was squalid, and ruined, like the first chaos, for which reason possibly he calls Judah the earth, in allusion to Gen. i, 2. The heavens - He seems to proceed in his metaphor of the chaos. Every thing above and below seemed to be wrapped up in dismal blackness.
Trembled — He proceeds in his figurative expressions. Behold how the very mountains of Judea tremble! Moved - As easily as dust, or feathers in a whirl-wind.
No man — All being either slain, or carried captive, or fled.
Yet — In the midst of judgment he will remember mercy.
Mourn — Expressions to set forth the dreadfulness of the judgment; he makes the elements to personate mourners.

glossa.text: *A burning wind. ((HIER.))* When, namely, the sword shall have reached unto the soul, etc., *as far as* by no means to the people, but to me shall it come, that my wheat may be scattered.

*A full spirit.* Certain men so expound this passage, that after the threshing-floor has been cleansed, the remnant may be saved. Whence it is written: *The spirit of fulness shall come to me;* whence the evangelist, *Of his fulness we all have received ((Joan. I))*. *And now I.* An aposiopesis, as Virgil says ((AENEID.)): Whom I *egos*; but it is better to settle the troubled waves.
The prophet, being about to speak prosperous things, holds himself back, and has joined sad things to sad.

*For my people is foolish. ((HIER.))* Because the princes of my people have not known, etc., *as far as* whom he ever desired to see? *They are wise,* etc. ((ID.)) Malicious wise men, etc., *as far as* it is called not wisdom, but craft and cunning.

*I beheld the earth.* The prophet discerns in spirit the things which are to come, that the people, hearing, may be terrified and do penance, that it may not suffer what it dreads. Whatever is said according to the history concerning Judaea and Jerusalem, let us refer to the Church of God: which, when it shall have offended God, and been laid waste by vices and by persecution, where once was the company of virtues and gladness, there may a multitude of sins and mourning be found.
*For thus saith. ((HIER.))* The clemency of the Lord is mingled with wrath: the land is forsaken, but it is not consumed, that there may remain those who understand his clemency .

*I have thought and have not repented,* etc. That I might take away the sentence foretold, and that the wrath of him that rages might not come to its end; the Lord threatened through Jonas, but the greatness of tears and groanings overcame the impending sword.

notes.text: The fool — The wicked man. Good - That is, actions really good or pleasing to God.

Looked — God knoweth all things without any enquiry: but he speaks after the manner of men. Upon - Upon the whole Israelitish nation, and upon all mankind for he speaks of all except his people, and the righteous ones, who are opposed to these, ver. 4, 5.
Gone — From God, and from the rule which he hath given them. Filthy - Loathsome and abominable to God.
Bread — With as little remorse, and with as much greediness. Call not - They are guilty not only of gross injustice towards men, but also of horrid impiety and contempt of God.
There — Upon the spot, where they practiced these insolences, God struck them with a panick fear. For - God is on their side, and therefore their enemies have cause to tremble.
Because — This was the ground of their contempt, that he lived by faith in God's promise and providence.

O that — These words immediately concern the deliverance of Israel out of that sinful state, in which they now were; which having described, he concludes, with a prayer to God to help them out of Zion, where the ark then was, but principally they design the spiritual redemption and salvation of all God's Israel by the Messiah. The captivity - His captive people. The children of Jacob, as Aaron is named for his sons, 1 Chron. xii, 27. The scope of this short, but excellent psalm, is to shew us the way to heaven. Here is a question proposed, ver. 1. The answer to it, ver. 2-5. A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *The fool hath said.* ((CASS.)) A rebuke of the Jews, their malice being described. The first psalm concerning the rebuke of the Jews, etc., *as far as* this man is not God.

*The Lord from heaven. ((Ibid.))* But from thence they are without excuse, because the Lord looked down, that is, he stood forth out of human nature. ((AUG.)) From heaven, that is, he looks down through holy souls: for by himself nothing lies hidden from him. Or, from heaven, through holy souls, which are the heaven and the seat of God. Or, the Lord the Father from heaven, that is, from the secret of the divine mind. ((CAS.)) Or, from the equality of God the Father. *If there be one that understandeth.* Or, he saw whether there be one that understandeth, and he found that not one understands: because he does not seek, but turns aside, for: *All have gone aside,* etc.

*A sepulchre. ((Ibid.))* Thus made useless to others, because their throat is a sepulchre, etc. *A sepulchre.* These three verses, which run as far as the second division, at *Shall they not know,* etc., are said not to be from the Hebrew, etc., *as far as* it does not have them.

*Destruction* ((AUG.)) Thus they have been made useless to themselves, etc., *as far as* and unhappiness in the time to come.

(CASS) The way of the wicked, etc., *as far as: The fear of God before their eyes,* etc.
*Shall they not know.* He threatens judgment to the wicked.

*The Lord they have not called upon,* etc. ((AUG.)) For they do not truly call upon him who love the things that displease God.--((CASS.)) Thence destruction is increased, because they must needs do evil, since the proud will not call upon God. As it is caution to fear at the fitting time, so it is cowardice to tremble unfittingly, as for nation and place, the fear of God being cast away.
*The counsel of the needy.* ((CASS.)) An invective against the Jews, etc., *as far as,* that is, proceeding from the Jews, etc.

*Who shall give out of Sion,* etc. ((CASS.)) Last of all the conversion of the Jews is foretold, which will come to pass when the fulness of the Gentiles has come in. *When he shall have turned away.* For the Jews too the Apostle sets down this testimony of Isaiah: *There shall come out of Sion he that turneth away the captivity, or the impiety, from Jacob.*

notes.text: I thank Christ, who hath enabled me, in that he accounted me faithful, having put me into the ministry — The meaning is, I thank him for putting me into the ministry, and enabling me to be faithful therein.

A blasphemer — Of Christ. A persecutor - Of his church. A reviler - Of his doctrine and people. But I obtained mercy - He does not say, because I was unconditionally elected; but because I did it in ignorance. Not that his ignorance took away his sin; but it left him capable of mercy; which he would hardly have been, had he acted thus contrary to his own conviction.
And the grace — Whereby I obtained mercy. Was exceeding abundant with faith - Opposite to my preceding unbelief. And love - Opposite to my blasphemy, persecution, and oppression.

This is a faithful saying — A most solemn preface. And worthy of all acceptation - Well deserving to be accepted, received, embraced, with all the faculties of our whole soul. That Christ - Promised. Jesus - Exhibited. Came into the world to save sinners - All sinners, without exception.
For this cause God showed me mercy, that all his longsuffering might be shown, and that none might hereafter despair.
The King of eternity — A phrase frequent with the Hebrews. How unspeakably sweet is the thought of eternity to believers!

glossa.text: *I give thanks to him who,* etc. Here he shows that evils had been his in the law. But the good things are these; [the evils] forgiven, that he is faithful, and placed in the ministry, whence also strong: by which things he shows that the law is uselessly drawn on after the Gospel.

*But the mercy of God.* Both they who sin knowingly, as David, and they who sin ignorantly, which is the more easily pardoned, obtain mercy. *I obtained mercy,* from this, that I did it ignorantly. Or ignorance is set down as the cause of mercy, yet not properly, since the ignorance was evil, but the mercy gratuitous.

*It hath superabounded.* Over greater goods than formerly evils. Because he not only forgave sins, but gave faith and love. Of which none must doubt: *That Jesus Christ came into this world to save sinners.* And this *word is faithful,* that is, true and acceptable, because useful.

*Of all acceptation,* because it saves both body and soul. Or, this word is human. Another reading: *That I say not divine,* because if a man who receives a man into his hospitality is called human, how much more human is he who receives man into himself. *Because Christ Jesus.* There was no cause of coming for Christ, save that he might save sinners.

*First.* That is, worse, because a persecutor, than whom there was none greater: For no one was fiercer among persecutors, therefore no one greater among sinners, he was first therefore not in order of time, but in greatness of iniquity.

*But for this cause mercy,* etc. Moreover he judges that for this cause he had obtained mercy, that no sinner now, pressed by whatsoever crimes, should despair of himself, but rather should presume by this example that he will obtain the same pardon: exceedingly great and truly vast is the gift. *In me.* Whom God appointed a fit preacher to the nations, in whom he showed forth so great an example of his mercy.

*Invisible.* Because the other gods are visible. It is not said *to the invisible alone,* because there are also certain invisible creatures, as the soul, which nevertheless can be apprehended by sense: because all its powers can be known, but it is not God to us. God, therefore, is invisible to men in his nature, according to that word: *No man hath seen God at any time.* But he is seen when he wills and as he wills, not as he is, but he wills to appear as it were in a form. But in the world to come the sons shall see him as he is. *To God alone.* Who alone is God by nature, that is, alone creates, which is understood of the Trinity itself, not of the Father alone, as some will have it: because he says not, to the Father alone, but to God alone. For the Trinity itself is preached by us as the one and only God. And the Only-begotten, according as he is God with God, and the Holy Spirit, is in his own nature immortal and invisible.

notes.text: All the publicans — That is, all who were in that place. It seems our Lord was in some town of Galilee of the Gentiles, from whence he afterward went to Jerusalem, chap. xvii, 11.

He spake — Three parables of the same import: for the sheep, the piece of silver, and the lost son, all declare (in direct contrariety to the Pharisees and scribes) in what manner God receiveth sinners.

Leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness — Where they used to feed: all uncultivated ground, like our commons, was by the Jews termed wilderness or desert. And go after - In recovering a lost soul, God as it were labours. May we not learn hence, that to let them alone who are in sin, is both unchristian and inhuman! Matt. xviii, 12.

Joy shall be — Solemn and festal joy, in heaven - First, in our blessed Lord himself, and then among the angels and spirits of just men, perhaps informed thereof by God himself, or by the angels who ministered to them. Over one sinner - One gross, open, notorious sinner, that repenteth - That is, thoroughly changed in heart and life; more than over ninety and nine just persons - Comparatively just, outwardly blameless: that need not such a repentance - For they need not, cannot repent of the sins which they never committed. The sum is, as a father peculiarly rejoices when an extravagant child, supposed to be utterly lost, comes to a thorough sense of his duty; or as any other person who has recovered what he had given up for gone, has a more sensible satisfaction in it, than in several other things equally valuable, but not in such danger: so do the angels in heaven peculiarly rejoice in the conversion of the most abandoned sinners. Yea, and God himself so readily forgives and receives them, that he may be represented as having part in the joy.

glossa.text:
*Who of you,* etc. In what went before thou hadst learned to renounce negligence, to shun arrogance, to take up devotion, not to be held fast by worldly occupations, not to prefer things that fall to things that abide. But because human frailty cannot keep a firm footing on so slippery a world, the physician there shows a remedy against error also, namely, that the judge does not deny the hope of pardon. *A hundred sheep.* Because the number of a hundred is a perfect number. God had a hundred sheep, that is, a perfect number, when he created the substance of angels and of men; but one perished, when man by sinning forsook the pastures of life: therefore, because the number of the rational creature was diminished by the perishing of man, he seeks man on earth that the sum may be made whole.

*Doth he not leave.* As if he said: You murmur, because I receive sinners, but I came not save to gather those going astray, as each one of you labours to bring back a straying sheep.

*He layeth it upon his shoulder.* He set the sheep upon his shoulders, who, taking up human nature, himself bore our sins: whence the shoulders of Christ are the arms of the cross; there he laid down our sins, on that neck of the noble gibbet he rested.

*And coming.* When man was repaired, the shepherd returns to heaven; there he finds the choirs of angels. They are friends, because in their steadfastness they keep his will continually; and they are neighbours, because they enjoy the brightness of his vision. And note that he does not say: Rejoice with the sheep that is found, but *with me,* because his joy is our life.

*I say to you.* In the ninety-nine, the number of the just is understood; in the one sheep, that of sinners. *Joy.* The angels, because they are rational, rejoice over a man reconciled to them, which sets us on fire toward uprightness: let us do what is pleasing to them, whose patronage we ought both to court and whose offence we ought to fear. *Than over.* If in the ninety-nine just who have not erred nor need penitence the angels are understood, it seems a greater thing to justify the impious than to create and preserve the just, because although each is of equal power, here there is greater mercy and greater joy.

*Or what woman.* The woman, that is, the Wisdom of God, had ten drachmas, when she created men and angels to her own image. But she lost one, when man withdrew from the likeness of his Creator. But the Wisdom of God kindled a lamp to seek with, when she appeared in the flesh, because a lamp is a light in an earthen vessel, that is, the Word in flesh. And when this shone forth among men, it overturned the house, because it troubled the consciences of men concerning their own guilt, and so the drachma is found again, while in man the likeness of the Maker is repaired. *Having ten drachmas.* The nature of angels and of men, which the Lord willed to subsist unto eternity, he created to his own likeness. Ten drachmas therefore the woman had, when to the nine orders of angels man was added, that the tenth number of the elect might be completed. And that number did not perish from its Creator even after the fault, because the Wisdom of God, flashing with miracles through the flesh, repaired it from the light of the earthen vessel. *She calleth together.* The friends and the neighbours are the powers above, which are near to God in the measure that they contemplate him more nearly. And she calls them, while through the showing of the grace bestowed upon men she kindles them more vehemently to the love of herself.

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
echoes.note: Paul's repeated 'I obtained mercy' draws on the LORD's self-revelation as merciful and gracious, slow to anger, the foundational OT confession of divine compassion. The mercy shown to the chief of sinners enacts this character of God. Exodus 34:6 is the wellspring of biblical mercy language.

echoes.text: Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom. Your dominion endures throughout all generations. Yahweh is faithful in all his words, and loving in all his deeds.
echoes.note: The doxology to 'the King eternal' draws on the Psalter's praise that 'your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom' and the LORD's dominion endures through all generations. Paul ascribes timeless kingship to the only God. Psalm 145 supplies the eternal-king acclamation.

echoes.text: Yahweh shall reign forever and ever.”
echoes.note: 'The King eternal' echoes the climactic acclamation of the Song of the Sea, 'The LORD shall reign forever and ever.' Paul's doxology takes up Israel's primal confession of God's everlasting reign. The Exodus hymn underlies the 'forever and ever' of the praise.

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.
echoes.note: 'The only God' (God who alone is wise / only God) is the Shema's confession that the LORD is one. Paul's monotheistic doxology rests on Israel's foundational creed. The Shema secures the 'only God' acclamation.

echoes.text: I will sow her to me in the earth; and I will have mercy on her who had not obtained mercy; and I will tell those who were not my people, ‘You are my people;’ and they will say, ‘My God!’”
echoes.note: Receiving mercy as one formerly outside it echoes Hosea's reversal where 'not pitied' becomes 'pitied' and the unloved become God's people. Paul the persecutor is the paradigm of unexpected mercy. The Hosea motif of mercy granted to the undeserving stands behind the testimony.

echoes.text: But you, Lord, are a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth.
echoes.note: Paul's mercy receives its texture from the Psalter's restatement of the Exodus 34 formula, 'a God merciful and gracious, abounding in steadfast love.' The grace that 'abounded exceedingly' resonates with this superabundant covenant mercy. A liturgical echo of the divine attributes.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to you out of the midst of the fire: you heard the voice of words, but you saw no form; you only heard a voice.
echoes.note: Calling God 'invisible' recalls Sinai, where Israel heard the voice but 'saw no form,' the basis of OT aniconism. Paul affirms the unseeable nature of the only God. Deuteronomy's no-form theology grounds the predicate 'invisible.'

echoes.text: I make a decree, that in all the dominion of my kingdom men tremble and fear before the God of Daniel; for he is the living God, and steadfast forever, His kingdom that which shall not be destroyed; and his dominion shall be even to the end.
echoes.note: Darius's decree that God 'is the living God, enduring forever; his kingdom shall never be destroyed' parallels Paul's praise of the King eternal and immortal. The Aramaic court tale supplies a Gentile confession of the everlasting, deathless God. A close conceptual model for the doxology.

echoes.text: And Tobit wrote a prayer for rejoicing, and said, “Blessed is God who lives forever! Blessed is his kingdom!
echoes.note: Tobit's hymn, 'Blessed be God who lives forever, for his kingdom lasts throughout all ages,' parallels the doxology's eternal, immortal King. The deuterocanonical doxology shares Paul's vocabulary of everlasting divine reign. Cited as a Second Temple liturgical analogue.

echoes.text: He that lives forever created all things in common.
echoes.note: 'He who lives forever created all things together' offers a deuterocanonical parallel to ascribing eternity and sole deity to God. The wisdom tradition's praise of the everliving Creator stands near Paul's doxology. A faint thematic echo from Second Temple piety.

echoes.text: “Come now, and let us reason together,” says Yahweh: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow. Though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
echoes.note: 'Christ came to save sinners' resonates with the prophetic invitation in which scarlet sins are made white as snow, the OT promise of cleansing for the guilty. Paul as foremost sinner receives this promised pardon. A contested thematic echo of prophetic forgiveness.

echoes.text: Unless Yahweh of Armies had left to us a very small remnant, we would have been as Sodom; we would have been like Gomorrah.
echoes.note: Paul's self-identification as 'foremost' of sinners yet shown mercy recalls the prophetic remnant spared by the LORD's grace despite Sodom-like guilt. The pattern of mercy preserving the unworthy underlies the testimony. Marked low as a diffuse echo.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: and in the morning, then you shall see Yahweh’s glory; because he hears your murmurings against Yahweh. Who are we, that you murmur against us?” Moses said, “Now Yahweh shall give you meat to eat in the evening, and in the morning bread to satisfy you; because Yahweh hears your murmurings which you murmur against him. And who are we? Your murmurings are not against us, but against Yahweh.”
echoes.note: The Pharisees and scribes 'murmured' (diegongyzon) that Jesus eats with sinners; LXX uses gongyzo precisely for Israel's murmuring against God's provision in the wilderness. Luke evokes the recurrent grumbling motif to cast the objectors as faithless Israel resisting God's gracious feeding. Coherence is strong because the parables that follow defend a divine table.

echoes.text: who say, Stand by yourself, don’t come near to me, for I am holier than you. These are a smoke in my nose, a fire that burns all the day.
echoes.note: The separatist who says 'Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am holier than you' supplies the exact posture Luke's Pharisees adopt against table fellowship with sinners. Isaiah condemns this self-segregating holiness as a stench before God, which coheres with Jesus' vindication of welcoming sinners. Availability and thematic coherence are high; verbal overlap is thematic rather than lexical.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;
echoes.note: The wisdom ideal that the righteous do not sit with sinners frames the Pharisees' assumption that eating with sinners defiles. Luke inverts the maxim: Jesus' table redefines blessedness as seeking rather than separating. Faint and contested, resting on shared sinner/righteous vocabulary.

echoes.text: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out. As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land; and I […]
echoes.note: God declares 'I myself will search for my sheep... I will seek the lost,' the precise plot of the one shepherd who leaves the flock to find the strayed (vv. 4,6,16). Volume is high (sustained seeking-shepherd oracle), recurrence strong (Ezekiel 34 is a touchstone for Luke's shepherd Christology), and coherence exact: God's own searching contrasts the failed shepherds, just as Jesus seeks sinners the Pharisees abandon.

echoes.text: He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.
echoes.note: The shepherd who gathers lambs and carries them in his bosom illuminates the man carrying the found sheep on his shoulders rejoicing. The tender carrying gesture is distinctive and shared, strengthening the divine-shepherd reading. Coheres with Ezekiel 34 as the comfort-of-God shepherd image.

echoes.text: I have gone astray like a lost sheep. Seek your servant, for I don’t forget your commandments.
echoes.note: 'I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant' supplies the penitent's voice answered by the seeking shepherd. The verbal pairing of straying sheep and divine seeking is close, and coherence with the repentance emphasis (v.7) is strong. Slightly lower volume than Ezekiel 34.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'All we like sheep have gone astray, we have turned every one to his own way' is the canonical image of straying that the parable assumes for 'one sinner who repents.' Recurrence in Luke's passion theology supports availability; the echo is thematic rather than cited here. Contested as to whether Luke intends the Servant song specifically.

echoes.text: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says Yahweh. Therefore thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, against the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them; behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings, says Yahweh. I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they […]
echoes.note: The woe on shepherds who scatter and the promise that God will gather the remnant and set true shepherds over them stands behind the lost-sheep rescue. Coheres with Ezekiel 34 as the prophetic indictment of leaders who fail the flock, paralleling the Pharisees. Lower volume, so an echo.

echoes.text: I will surely assemble, Jacob, all of you; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as a flock in the midst of their pasture; they will swarm with people.
echoes.note: God's promise to gather the remnant of Israel 'like sheep in a fold' supplies the regathering motif. Faint and one of several gathering oracles; included for recurrence within the shepherd-restoration cluster. Contested because no distinctive verbal link to a single lost sheep.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh my God: “Feed the flock of slaughter. Their buyers slaughter them, and go unpunished. Those who sell them say, ‘Blessed be Yahweh, for I am rich;’ and their own shepherds don’t pity them. For I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land,” says Yahweh; “but, behold, I will deliver the men everyone into his neighbor’s hand, and into the hand of his king. They will strike the land, and out of their hand I will not deliver them.” So I fed […]
echoes.note: The flock doomed to slaughter and the shepherd's care/abandonment drama belongs to the same prophetic shepherd field Luke draws on. Faint here; included as availability for the seeking-shepherd theme. Contested.

echoes.text: It will happen at that time, that I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and I will punish the men who are settled on their dregs, who say in their heart, “Yahweh will not do good, neither will he do evil.”
echoes.note: God 'searches Jerusalem with lamps' to find the complacent, a near image to the woman lighting a lamp and sweeping to find the coin. The lamp-search vocabulary is suggestive, though Zephaniah's search is judicial, here gracious. Contested and faint.

echoes.text: If you seek her as silver, and search for her as for hidden treasures:
echoes.note: Seeking wisdom 'as silver, and searching for it as for hidden treasure' parallels the diligent search for the lost silver drachma until found. The seek-until-found wisdom pattern coheres with the parable's diligence, but the link is thematic. Contested.

echoes.text: By night on my bed, I sought him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but I didn’t find him. I will get up now, and go about the city; in the streets and in the squares I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but I didn’t find him. The watchmen who go about the city found me; “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” I had scarcely passed from them, when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him […]
echoes.note: The beloved who seeks through the night 'until I found him' and then summons others to rejoice mirrors the woman's seek-find-celebrate structure. Faint, figural, contested; included as a seek-and-find availability rather than a deliberate citation.

notes.text: They have turned aside quickly — Quickly after the law was given them, and they had promised to obey it; quickly after God had done such great things for them, and declared his kind intentions to do greater.
It is a stiff-necked people — Unapt to come under the yoke of the divine law, averse to all good, and prone to evil, obstinate to the methods of cure.

Let me alone — What did Moses, or what could he do, to hinder God from consuming them? When God resolves to abandon a people, and the decree is gone forth, no intercession can prevent it. But God would thus express the greatness of his displeasure, after the manner of men, who would have none to interceed for those they resolve to be severe with. Thus also he would put an honour upon prayer, intimating, that nothing but the intercession of Moses could save them from ruin, that he might be a type of Christ, by whose mediation alone God would reconcile the world unto himself.

And Moses besought the Lord his God — If God would not be called the God of Israel, yet he hoped he might address him as his own God. Now Moses is standing in the gap to turn away the wrath of God. Psalm cvi, 23. He took the hint which God gave him when he said, Let me alone, which, though it seemed to forbid his interceding, did really encourage it, by shewing what power the prayer of faith hath with God.

Turn from thy fierce wrath — Not as if he thought God were not justly angry, but he begs that he would not be so greatly angry as to consume them. Let mercy rejoice against judgment; repent of this evil - Change the sentence of destruction into that of correction, against thy people which thou broughtest up out of Egypt - For whom thou hast done so great things? Wherefore should the Egyptians say, For mischief did he bring them out - Israel is dear to Moses, as his kindred, as his charge; but it is the glory of God that he is most concerned for. If Israel could perish without any reproach to God's name, Moses could persuade himself to sit down contented; but he cannot bear to hear God reflected on; and therefore this he insists upon, Lord, What will the Egyptians say? They will say, God was either weak, and could not, or fickle, and would not compleat the salvation he begun.
Remember Abraham — Lord, if Israel be cut off, what will become of the promise?

And the Lord repented of the evil he thought to do — Though he designed to punish them, yet he would not ruin them. See here, the power of prayer, God suffers himself to be prevailed with by humble believing importunity. And see the compassion of God towards poor sinners, and how ready he is to forgive.

glossa.text: *These are thy gods. ((AUG., quaest. 142.))* The Lord, showing to Moses what the people had done concerning the calf and concerning the idol which they had made out of their own gold, says that they had said: These are thy gods, O Israel, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt. Which it is not read that they said; but God showed that this was their mind, for they bore in their heart the sense of these words, which could not lie hid from God.

*Let me alone,* etc. ((GREG., lib. IX Moral., cap. 11.)) What is it to say to a servant, etc., *as far as* he could not temper the anger of God for himself.

((ID., lib. XX Moral., cap. 6.)) It can build up the reader according to the history, etc., *as far as* nor mercy of discipline.

*Remember Abraham, Isaac,* etc. He brings in the fathers, who are loved, on behalf of the sons, who offend, and do not deserve to be heard; because the good things of the holy fathers often come to the aid of the sons.

*And the Lord was appeased that he would not do the evil.* ((AUG.)) By malice he wished punishment to be understood here, as is that: The malice of their going out was esteemed. According to this both good and evil are said to be from God, not according to the malice by which men are evil. For God is not evil: but he brings evils upon the evil, because he is just.

notes.text: Thee only — Which is not to be, understood absolutely, because he had sinned against Bathsheba and Uriah, and many others; but comparatively. So the sense is, though I have sinned against my own conscience, and against others; yet nothing is more grievous to me, than that I have sinned against thee. Thy sight - With gross contempt of thee, whom I knew to be a spectator of my most secret actions. Justified - This will be the fruit of my sin, that whatsoever severities thou shalt use towards me, it will be no blemish to thy righteousness, but thy justice will be glorified by all men. Speakest - Hebrew. in thy words, in all thy threatenings denounced against me. Judgest - When thou dost execute thy sentence upon me.

Behold — Nor is this the only sin which I have reason to bewail before thee; for this filthy stream leads me to a corrupt fountain: and upon a review of my heart, I find, that this heinous crime, was the proper fruit of my vile nature, which, ever was, and still is ready to commit ten thousand sins, as occasion offers.

Truth — Uprightness of heart; and this may be added; as an aggravation of the sinfulness of original corruption, because it is contrary to the holy nature and will of God, which requires rectitude of heart: and, as an aggravation of his actual sin, that it was committed against that knowledge, which God had wrote in his heart.

Hyssop — As lepers, are by thy appointment purified by the use of hyssop and other things, so do thou cleanse me a leprous and polluted creature, by thy grace, and by that blood of Christ, which is signified by those ceremonial usages.
Joy — By thy spirit, seal the pardon of my sins on my conscience, which will fill me with joy. Rejoice - That my heart which hath been sorely wounded may be comforted.

Create — Work in me an holy frame of heart, whereby my inward filth may be purged away. Right - Hebrew. firm or constant, that my resolution may be fixed and unmoveable. Spirit - Temper or disposition of soul.

glossa.text: *Unto the end, a psalm.* ((CASS.)) When Nathan rebuked him, the king did not blush to confess his sins publicly, etc., *as far as* what avails with God for the penitent. *Of David.* ((AUG.)) He is set forth as an example, not of falling, but of rising again if thou hast fallen, that thou despair not. ((CASS.)) The first thing is entreaty, etc., *as far as* full remission of sins is granted.

*Have mercy on me, O God. ((Ibid.))* This is a penitential psalm, etc., *as far as* because he foresaw that through this psalm many would perish. *According to thy great mercy.* Of a grave sin one would have to despair, were there not a great mercy *misericodia*. A great one cannot be defined, how great it is. *Great mercy. ((Ibid.))* A great mercy brought God down from heaven, etc., *as far as* when God is asked to pardon according to himself? *Of thy tender mercies,* etc. ((CASS.)) He asks through mercy and through tender mercy. And mercy is in the nature, tender mercy in the effect.

*Wash me yet more.* ((CASS.)) What manner of blotting out he would have, he adds: *Cleanse me,* etc. ((HIER.)) So wash that thou make clean; for certain things are washed which nevertheless are not pure.

*For iniquity.* ((AUG., CASS.)) Whose mercy he asks that he may pardon, because he knows him just, that he punishes sins, he adds: Punish thou not, because I punish. *For my iniquity,* etc. *Against me.* ((AUG.)) He had his sin behind his back, when the king gave sentence against the rich man who had seized the poor man's ewe, forgetful of himself.

*To thee only have I sinned.* ((HIER.)) For he alone punishes justly who has not in himself anything that may be reproved; and among men this is Christ alone. *To thee only.* ((CASS.)) Because a king is superior to all, he is to be punished by God alone. *Before thee.* Because he knows that he is everywhere; whence he accuses himself, because in his presence he did not blush to sin. *That thou mayest be justified,* etc. Whose words do not pass away, but are fulfilled. *And mayest overcome when thou art judged.* God is of such great justice *t antae*, etc., *as far as* that he may overcome as between himself and him, if they be judged.

*To thee only.* ((AUG.)) To Christ, who had no sin, etc., *as far as* in that he had so grievously offended God. *And mayest overcome.* ((AUG.)) Or, thou art so just that thou overcomest the devil, and death, and the Jews, when thou art judged: and in the judgment wherein thou wast judged.
*In iniquities.* ((CASS.)) The odium of the sin is lessened, etc., *as far as* he is accused of one and confesses all.

*For behold,* etc. ((AUG.)) He so gives mercy that he keeps truth, so that not even the sins of him whom he pardons are unpunished. For he pardons the man who punishes himself. Mercy therefore it is that a man is set free; truth, that the sin is punished. *Truth,* etc. ((CASS.)) Because in confessing he spoke the truth, which God seeks above sacrifices, he entreats that help be brought him. *The uncertain and hidden things.* ((AUG.)) There are hidden things also, in that to such men, etc., *as far as* whence he had the more to beware of sin. *The hidden things.* ((CASS.)) From the authority of him who makes them manifest, the confidence of washing and of being made white.

*Thou shalt sprinkle me.* ((CASS.)) The second thing is confidence in the mercy of God, which is very profitable: lest despair creep in, which is graver than all sins. *With hyssop. ((Ibid.))* Dipped in the blood of the victim, it was sprinkled over the body of the leper, signifying that the stains of sins are to be washed away by the blood of Christ. ((AUG.)) Hyssop is a lowly herb, etc., *as far as* in which there is a swelling, so humility, pride. *Above snow. ((Ibid.))* Incomparably: whence also on the mountain the garment of Christ shone as snow.
*To my hearing.* ((AUG.)) Mark the humble man. Let me hear thee, etc., *as far as* and because he is now humble, now *the bones that were humbled rejoice.*

notes.text: I thank Christ, who hath enabled me, in that he accounted me faithful, having put me into the ministry — The meaning is, I thank him for putting me into the ministry, and enabling me to be faithful therein.

A blasphemer — Of Christ. A persecutor - Of his church. A reviler - Of his doctrine and people. But I obtained mercy - He does not say, because I was unconditionally elected; but because I did it in ignorance. Not that his ignorance took away his sin; but it left him capable of mercy; which he would hardly have been, had he acted thus contrary to his own conviction.
And the grace — Whereby I obtained mercy. Was exceeding abundant with faith - Opposite to my preceding unbelief. And love - Opposite to my blasphemy, persecution, and oppression.

This is a faithful saying — A most solemn preface. And worthy of all acceptation - Well deserving to be accepted, received, embraced, with all the faculties of our whole soul. That Christ - Promised. Jesus - Exhibited. Came into the world to save sinners - All sinners, without exception.
For this cause God showed me mercy, that all his longsuffering might be shown, and that none might hereafter despair.
The King of eternity — A phrase frequent with the Hebrews. How unspeakably sweet is the thought of eternity to believers!

glossa.text: *I give thanks to him who,* etc. Here he shows that evils had been his in the law. But the good things are these; [the evils] forgiven, that he is faithful, and placed in the ministry, whence also strong: by which things he shows that the law is uselessly drawn on after the Gospel.

*But the mercy of God.* Both they who sin knowingly, as David, and they who sin ignorantly, which is the more easily pardoned, obtain mercy. *I obtained mercy,* from this, that I did it ignorantly. Or ignorance is set down as the cause of mercy, yet not properly, since the ignorance was evil, but the mercy gratuitous.

*It hath superabounded.* Over greater goods than formerly evils. Because he not only forgave sins, but gave faith and love. Of which none must doubt: *That Jesus Christ came into this world to save sinners.* And this *word is faithful,* that is, true and acceptable, because useful.

*Of all acceptation,* because it saves both body and soul. Or, this word is human. Another reading: *That I say not divine,* because if a man who receives a man into his hospitality is called human, how much more human is he who receives man into himself. *Because Christ Jesus.* There was no cause of coming for Christ, save that he might save sinners.

*First.* That is, worse, because a persecutor, than whom there was none greater: For no one was fiercer among persecutors, therefore no one greater among sinners, he was first therefore not in order of time, but in greatness of iniquity.

*But for this cause mercy,* etc. Moreover he judges that for this cause he had obtained mercy, that no sinner now, pressed by whatsoever crimes, should despair of himself, but rather should presume by this example that he will obtain the same pardon: exceedingly great and truly vast is the gift. *In me.* Whom God appointed a fit preacher to the nations, in whom he showed forth so great an example of his mercy.

*Invisible.* Because the other gods are visible. It is not said *to the invisible alone,* because there are also certain invisible creatures, as the soul, which nevertheless can be apprehended by sense: because all its powers can be known, but it is not God to us. God, therefore, is invisible to men in his nature, according to that word: *No man hath seen God at any time.* But he is seen when he wills and as he wills, not as he is, but he wills to appear as it were in a form. But in the world to come the sons shall see him as he is. *To God alone.* Who alone is God by nature, that is, alone creates, which is understood of the Trinity itself, not of the Father alone, as some will have it: because he says not, to the Father alone, but to God alone. For the Trinity itself is preached by us as the one and only God. And the Only-begotten, according as he is God with God, and the Holy Spirit, is in his own nature immortal and invisible.

notes.text: All the publicans — That is, all who were in that place. It seems our Lord was in some town of Galilee of the Gentiles, from whence he afterward went to Jerusalem, chap. xvii, 11.

He spake — Three parables of the same import: for the sheep, the piece of silver, and the lost son, all declare (in direct contrariety to the Pharisees and scribes) in what manner God receiveth sinners.

Leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness — Where they used to feed: all uncultivated ground, like our commons, was by the Jews termed wilderness or desert. And go after - In recovering a lost soul, God as it were labours. May we not learn hence, that to let them alone who are in sin, is both unchristian and inhuman! Matt. xviii, 12.

Joy shall be — Solemn and festal joy, in heaven - First, in our blessed Lord himself, and then among the angels and spirits of just men, perhaps informed thereof by God himself, or by the angels who ministered to them. Over one sinner - One gross, open, notorious sinner, that repenteth - That is, thoroughly changed in heart and life; more than over ninety and nine just persons - Comparatively just, outwardly blameless: that need not such a repentance - For they need not, cannot repent of the sins which they never committed. The sum is, as a father peculiarly rejoices when an extravagant child, supposed to be utterly lost, comes to a thorough sense of his duty; or as any other person who has recovered what he had given up for gone, has a more sensible satisfaction in it, than in several other things equally valuable, but not in such danger: so do the angels in heaven peculiarly rejoice in the conversion of the most abandoned sinners. Yea, and God himself so readily forgives and receives them, that he may be represented as having part in the joy.

glossa.text:
*Who of you,* etc. In what went before thou hadst learned to renounce negligence, to shun arrogance, to take up devotion, not to be held fast by worldly occupations, not to prefer things that fall to things that abide. But because human frailty cannot keep a firm footing on so slippery a world, the physician there shows a remedy against error also, namely, that the judge does not deny the hope of pardon. *A hundred sheep.* Because the number of a hundred is a perfect number. God had a hundred sheep, that is, a perfect number, when he created the substance of angels and of men; but one perished, when man by sinning forsook the pastures of life: therefore, because the number of the rational creature was diminished by the perishing of man, he seeks man on earth that the sum may be made whole.

*Doth he not leave.* As if he said: You murmur, because I receive sinners, but I came not save to gather those going astray, as each one of you labours to bring back a straying sheep.

*He layeth it upon his shoulder.* He set the sheep upon his shoulders, who, taking up human nature, himself bore our sins: whence the shoulders of Christ are the arms of the cross; there he laid down our sins, on that neck of the noble gibbet he rested.

*And coming.* When man was repaired, the shepherd returns to heaven; there he finds the choirs of angels. They are friends, because in their steadfastness they keep his will continually; and they are neighbours, because they enjoy the brightness of his vision. And note that he does not say: Rejoice with the sheep that is found, but *with me,* because his joy is our life.

*I say to you.* In the ninety-nine, the number of the just is understood; in the one sheep, that of sinners. *Joy.* The angels, because they are rational, rejoice over a man reconciled to them, which sets us on fire toward uprightness: let us do what is pleasing to them, whose patronage we ought both to court and whose offence we ought to fear. *Than over.* If in the ninety-nine just who have not erred nor need penitence the angels are understood, it seems a greater thing to justify the impious than to create and preserve the just, because although each is of equal power, here there is greater mercy and greater joy.

*Or what woman.* The woman, that is, the Wisdom of God, had ten drachmas, when she created men and angels to her own image. But she lost one, when man withdrew from the likeness of his Creator. But the Wisdom of God kindled a lamp to seek with, when she appeared in the flesh, because a lamp is a light in an earthen vessel, that is, the Word in flesh. And when this shone forth among men, it overturned the house, because it troubled the consciences of men concerning their own guilt, and so the drachma is found again, while in man the likeness of the Maker is repaired. *Having ten drachmas.* The nature of angels and of men, which the Lord willed to subsist unto eternity, he created to his own likeness. Ten drachmas therefore the woman had, when to the nine orders of angels man was added, that the tenth number of the elect might be completed. And that number did not perish from its Creator even after the fault, because the Wisdom of God, flashing with miracles through the flesh, repaired it from the light of the earthen vessel. *She calleth together.* The friends and the neighbours are the powers above, which are near to God in the measure that they contemplate him more nearly. And she calls them, while through the showing of the grace bestowed upon men she kindles them more vehemently to the love of herself.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)
Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
echoes.note: Paul's repeated 'I obtained mercy' draws on the LORD's self-revelation as merciful and gracious, slow to anger, the foundational OT confession of divine compassion. The mercy shown to the chief of sinners enacts this character of God. Exodus 34:6 is the wellspring of biblical mercy language.

echoes.text: Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom. Your dominion endures throughout all generations. Yahweh is faithful in all his words, and loving in all his deeds.
echoes.note: The doxology to 'the King eternal' draws on the Psalter's praise that 'your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom' and the LORD's dominion endures through all generations. Paul ascribes timeless kingship to the only God. Psalm 145 supplies the eternal-king acclamation.

echoes.text: Yahweh shall reign forever and ever.”
echoes.note: 'The King eternal' echoes the climactic acclamation of the Song of the Sea, 'The LORD shall reign forever and ever.' Paul's doxology takes up Israel's primal confession of God's everlasting reign. The Exodus hymn underlies the 'forever and ever' of the praise.

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.
echoes.note: 'The only God' (God who alone is wise / only God) is the Shema's confession that the LORD is one. Paul's monotheistic doxology rests on Israel's foundational creed. The Shema secures the 'only God' acclamation.

echoes.text: I will sow her to me in the earth; and I will have mercy on her who had not obtained mercy; and I will tell those who were not my people, ‘You are my people;’ and they will say, ‘My God!’”
echoes.note: Receiving mercy as one formerly outside it echoes Hosea's reversal where 'not pitied' becomes 'pitied' and the unloved become God's people. Paul the persecutor is the paradigm of unexpected mercy. The Hosea motif of mercy granted to the undeserving stands behind the testimony.

echoes.text: But you, Lord, are a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth.
echoes.note: Paul's mercy receives its texture from the Psalter's restatement of the Exodus 34 formula, 'a God merciful and gracious, abounding in steadfast love.' The grace that 'abounded exceedingly' resonates with this superabundant covenant mercy. A liturgical echo of the divine attributes.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to you out of the midst of the fire: you heard the voice of words, but you saw no form; you only heard a voice.
echoes.note: Calling God 'invisible' recalls Sinai, where Israel heard the voice but 'saw no form,' the basis of OT aniconism. Paul affirms the unseeable nature of the only God. Deuteronomy's no-form theology grounds the predicate 'invisible.'

echoes.text: I make a decree, that in all the dominion of my kingdom men tremble and fear before the God of Daniel; for he is the living God, and steadfast forever, His kingdom that which shall not be destroyed; and his dominion shall be even to the end.
echoes.note: Darius's decree that God 'is the living God, enduring forever; his kingdom shall never be destroyed' parallels Paul's praise of the King eternal and immortal. The Aramaic court tale supplies a Gentile confession of the everlasting, deathless God. A close conceptual model for the doxology.

echoes.text: And Tobit wrote a prayer for rejoicing, and said, “Blessed is God who lives forever! Blessed is his kingdom!
echoes.note: Tobit's hymn, 'Blessed be God who lives forever, for his kingdom lasts throughout all ages,' parallels the doxology's eternal, immortal King. The deuterocanonical doxology shares Paul's vocabulary of everlasting divine reign. Cited as a Second Temple liturgical analogue.

echoes.text: He that lives forever created all things in common.
echoes.note: 'He who lives forever created all things together' offers a deuterocanonical parallel to ascribing eternity and sole deity to God. The wisdom tradition's praise of the everliving Creator stands near Paul's doxology. A faint thematic echo from Second Temple piety.

echoes.text: “Come now, and let us reason together,” says Yahweh: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow. Though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
echoes.note: 'Christ came to save sinners' resonates with the prophetic invitation in which scarlet sins are made white as snow, the OT promise of cleansing for the guilty. Paul as foremost sinner receives this promised pardon. A contested thematic echo of prophetic forgiveness.

echoes.text: Unless Yahweh of Armies had left to us a very small remnant, we would have been as Sodom; we would have been like Gomorrah.
echoes.note: Paul's self-identification as 'foremost' of sinners yet shown mercy recalls the prophetic remnant spared by the LORD's grace despite Sodom-like guilt. The pattern of mercy preserving the unworthy underlies the testimony. Marked low as a diffuse echo.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: and in the morning, then you shall see Yahweh’s glory; because he hears your murmurings against Yahweh. Who are we, that you murmur against us?” Moses said, “Now Yahweh shall give you meat to eat in the evening, and in the morning bread to satisfy you; because Yahweh hears your murmurings which you murmur against him. And who are we? Your murmurings are not against us, but against Yahweh.”
echoes.note: The Pharisees and scribes 'murmured' (diegongyzon) that Jesus eats with sinners; LXX uses gongyzo precisely for Israel's murmuring against God's provision in the wilderness. Luke evokes the recurrent grumbling motif to cast the objectors as faithless Israel resisting God's gracious feeding. Coherence is strong because the parables that follow defend a divine table.

echoes.text: who say, Stand by yourself, don’t come near to me, for I am holier than you. These are a smoke in my nose, a fire that burns all the day.
echoes.note: The separatist who says 'Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am holier than you' supplies the exact posture Luke's Pharisees adopt against table fellowship with sinners. Isaiah condemns this self-segregating holiness as a stench before God, which coheres with Jesus' vindication of welcoming sinners. Availability and thematic coherence are high; verbal overlap is thematic rather than lexical.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;
echoes.note: The wisdom ideal that the righteous do not sit with sinners frames the Pharisees' assumption that eating with sinners defiles. Luke inverts the maxim: Jesus' table redefines blessedness as seeking rather than separating. Faint and contested, resting on shared sinner/righteous vocabulary.

echoes.text: For thus says the Lord Yahweh: Behold, I myself, even I, will search for my sheep, and will seek them out. As a shepherd seeks out his flock in the day that he is among his sheep that are scattered abroad, so will I seek out my sheep; and I will deliver them out of all places where they have been scattered in the cloudy and dark day. I will bring them out from the peoples, and gather them from the countries, and will bring them into their own land; and I […]
echoes.note: God declares 'I myself will search for my sheep... I will seek the lost,' the precise plot of the one shepherd who leaves the flock to find the strayed (vv. 4,6,16). Volume is high (sustained seeking-shepherd oracle), recurrence strong (Ezekiel 34 is a touchstone for Luke's shepherd Christology), and coherence exact: God's own searching contrasts the failed shepherds, just as Jesus seeks sinners the Pharisees abandon.

echoes.text: He will feed his flock like a shepherd. He will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom. He will gently lead those who have their young.
echoes.note: The shepherd who gathers lambs and carries them in his bosom illuminates the man carrying the found sheep on his shoulders rejoicing. The tender carrying gesture is distinctive and shared, strengthening the divine-shepherd reading. Coheres with Ezekiel 34 as the comfort-of-God shepherd image.

echoes.text: I have gone astray like a lost sheep. Seek your servant, for I don’t forget your commandments.
echoes.note: 'I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant' supplies the penitent's voice answered by the seeking shepherd. The verbal pairing of straying sheep and divine seeking is close, and coherence with the repentance emphasis (v.7) is strong. Slightly lower volume than Ezekiel 34.

echoes.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'All we like sheep have gone astray, we have turned every one to his own way' is the canonical image of straying that the parable assumes for 'one sinner who repents.' Recurrence in Luke's passion theology supports availability; the echo is thematic rather than cited here. Contested as to whether Luke intends the Servant song specifically.

echoes.text: Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture! says Yahweh. Therefore thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, against the shepherds who feed my people: You have scattered my flock, and driven them away, and have not visited them; behold, I will visit on you the evil of your doings, says Yahweh. I will gather the remnant of my flock out of all the countries where I have driven them, and will bring them again to their folds; and they […]
echoes.note: The woe on shepherds who scatter and the promise that God will gather the remnant and set true shepherds over them stands behind the lost-sheep rescue. Coheres with Ezekiel 34 as the prophetic indictment of leaders who fail the flock, paralleling the Pharisees. Lower volume, so an echo.

echoes.text: I will surely assemble, Jacob, all of you; I will surely gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as a flock in the midst of their pasture; they will swarm with people.
echoes.note: God's promise to gather the remnant of Israel 'like sheep in a fold' supplies the regathering motif. Faint and one of several gathering oracles; included for recurrence within the shepherd-restoration cluster. Contested because no distinctive verbal link to a single lost sheep.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh my God: “Feed the flock of slaughter. Their buyers slaughter them, and go unpunished. Those who sell them say, ‘Blessed be Yahweh, for I am rich;’ and their own shepherds don’t pity them. For I will no more pity the inhabitants of the land,” says Yahweh; “but, behold, I will deliver the men everyone into his neighbor’s hand, and into the hand of his king. They will strike the land, and out of their hand I will not deliver them.” So I fed […]
echoes.note: The flock doomed to slaughter and the shepherd's care/abandonment drama belongs to the same prophetic shepherd field Luke draws on. Faint here; included as availability for the seeking-shepherd theme. Contested.

echoes.text: It will happen at that time, that I will search Jerusalem with lamps, and I will punish the men who are settled on their dregs, who say in their heart, “Yahweh will not do good, neither will he do evil.”
echoes.note: God 'searches Jerusalem with lamps' to find the complacent, a near image to the woman lighting a lamp and sweeping to find the coin. The lamp-search vocabulary is suggestive, though Zephaniah's search is judicial, here gracious. Contested and faint.

echoes.text: If you seek her as silver, and search for her as for hidden treasures:
echoes.note: Seeking wisdom 'as silver, and searching for it as for hidden treasure' parallels the diligent search for the lost silver drachma until found. The seek-until-found wisdom pattern coheres with the parable's diligence, but the link is thematic. Contested.

echoes.text: By night on my bed, I sought him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but I didn’t find him. I will get up now, and go about the city; in the streets and in the squares I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but I didn’t find him. The watchmen who go about the city found me; “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” I had scarcely passed from them, when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him […]
echoes.note: The beloved who seeks through the night 'until I found him' and then summons others to rejoice mirrors the woman's seek-find-celebrate structure. Faint, figural, contested; included as a seek-and-find availability rather than a deliberate citation.

registers.label: Spare
lines: One sheep wandered off, and the shepherd left the ninety-nine to find it.
He lays it on his shoulders and carries it home rejoicing.
A woman lit a lamp and swept the house until the lost coin gleamed.
Rejoice with me; what was lost is found.
Christ Jesus came to save sinners, and we are not too far gone for grace.
Mercy reached the worst of us; mercy reaches us still.
Come, you who were found, and worship.
There is joy in heaven over us. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Picture a woman on her knees with a lamp, sweeping every corner of a dark house, fingers brushing the floor for one small coin.
Rejoice with me; what was lost is found.
And when it catches the light at last, she does not pocket it quietly — she runs to the neighbors, calling everyone to be glad.
Rejoice with me; what was lost is found.
So it is with the shepherd and the strayed sheep, hoisted onto his shoulders and carried home; so it is in heaven over one who turns back.
Rejoice with me; what was lost is found.
However far off you have felt this week, hear this: Christ came for sinners, and mercy has come looking for you. You are found.
Rejoice with me; what was lost is found. Thanks be to God!
